title: Negotiating AI Limits and Biological Weapons
content:
Earlier this month, US researchers used AI to design new viruses for the first time. Though these viruses were created only to combat bacteria like E. coli, the breakthrough has led to increased calls for international agreements to regulate the use of AI to develop biological weapons.

However, one drawback of our current unipolar moment is that the US has become unaccustomed to negotiating formal agreements with its opponents. In any case, there is currently a lack of interest in formal agreements. 

What would it take to actually get agreement on AI?

First, there must be a shared perception of risk and threat. The Cuban Missile Crisis inspired a generation of agreements for nuclear weapons, conventional military action, and WMD. Leaders in both Russia and the United States remembered their experiences in World War II and feared the return of global war fueled by nuclear weapons. This common understanding created the basis for negotiation and, ultimately, agreement.

title: Southeast Asia Shows Surprising Semiconductor Strengths
content:
It’s the indispensable back end of the Western semiconductor stack. Malaysia, the Philippines, and Singapore form a critical trio for the assembly, testing, and advanced packaging of semiconductors.

The Southeast Asian trio does not aim to replicate Taiwanese-style leading‑edge fabs. They are doubling down on their existing back‑end strengths and upgrading their skills to service automotive, defense, and AI chips. For all three countries, semiconductors represent a key industry, and each specializes in a specific part of the value chain. 

The Philippines, the least-developed economy of the three, leverages its English-speaking technical workforce. Multinational chipmakers including Intel, Texas Instruments, and Analog Devices run large Filipino operations. They import raw wafers to assemble, package, and test. 

The economic impact is immense. Electronics account for almost 60% of the Philippines’ goods exports, with about three-quarters, or about $31 billion per year, attributable to semiconductors.
snippet: It’s the indispensable back end of the Western semiconductor stack. Malaysia, the Philippines, and Singapore form a critical trio for the assembly, testing, and advanced packaging of semiconductors.

title: When You Talk To Your Pet Brick, Does It Talk Back? AI’s Cult of Personality
content:
The human tendency to assign personality to objects or machines goes back millennia, with people anthropomorphizing their ships, swords, or cars. For centuries, people have been naming objects, talking to them, and attributing individual quirks to them. It’s poetic, but imaginary. Giving something a name and talking to it does not make it human. 
 
Attributing personality to a device is different from a device actually having a personality, and this has become a problem in discussions around AI. Maybe it’s just the headline writers, but AI does not “escape” or “go rogue.” Instead, it’s an engineering problem. 
 
Look at self-driving cars; they’re imperfect, but improving. They make mistakes when they stop suddenly, run over pedestrians, or are unable to select what set of instructions to execute in a power outage. But no one says a Tesla “went rogue” when its program fails to recognize a stop sign, because these terms imply intent.

title: Lukashenka’s ‘Capitulation’ to Zelenskyy’s Ultimatum
content:
Since January, Ukraine has noticeably hardened its public tone toward Belarus. This toughened rhetoric culminated on June 19 in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s ultimatum to the Belarusian leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka. 

The Ukrainian president gave Minsk a week to deactivate Russian signal boosters on Belarusian territory used to control drones heading toward Ukraine. Zelenskyy added: “If he does not do it, we will.”

Although Lukashenka initially responded to Zelenskyy with his own military threats and personal insults, the Belarusian leader ultimately yielded to Kyiv’s demands. According to Ukrainian intelligence reports, Minsk deactivated the drone control systems on June 22. 

On closer inspection, however, Lukashenka’s about-face had actually taken place a week before he gave in — and four days prior to Zelenskyy’s ultimatum. title: Trump’s Route Begins to Re-Make the South Caucasus
content:
August marks the first anniversary of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) – an agreement poised to reshape the geopolitics of the South Caucasus. 

On the map, the scale of the project (about 42 km, or 26 miles) might not be staggering. But the route is laden with political and geographic meaning as a link between former warring states, connecting Azerbaijan proper and its exclave of Nakhchivan via Armenia’s southernmost territory of Syunik. That opens possibilities for further east-west routes to Turkey’s Mediterranean coast and beyond the Caspian Sea. It also tramples on what the Kremlin imagines to be its backyard.

The route is likely to include road, rail, data, and energy pipelines. Over the past year, the signatories agreed on surveying work for the railway element that will include a link to Turkey. The sides also agreed to establish a Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund with a capitalization of $201m.
snippet: August marks the first anniversary of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) – an agreement poised to reshape the geopolitics of the South Caucasus.

title: Data Centers Move Center Stage
content:
In Virginia, home to the world’s largest concentration of data centers, the buildout of AI data centers has become a central campaign issue. In Finland, public anger is rising over grid strain.

It’s a common European and American challenge: how to confront a political backlash against rapid AI infrastructure expansion. Voters are rebelling against rising utility costs — and their anxieties over AI. A recent Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans are against data center construction, and 39% of those surveyed by Pew Research Center consider data centers to be “mostly bad” for the environment.

European polls report similar large majorities in favor of reigning in expansion. Bills banning data center construction have been proposed in 15 states, in both Republican and Democratic strongholds — while in Europe, moratoriums and connection grid freezes are proliferating.

title: Ukrainians Embrace God but Shun Moscow Orthodoxy
content:
Polling suggests the war has made Ukrainians more religious. But a closer look at more than two decades of data suggests a more complex picture.

While 12 years of Russian aggression have strengthened religious commitment among a significant minority of Ukrainians, the relationship between religious faith, church affiliation, and national identity has changed dramatically.

The share of Ukrainians describing themselves as believers increased to 71% in 2010, from 58% in 2000, according to Razumkov Centre research. Between 2010 and 2020, the share remained around 70%, though it rose during periods of crisis, to 76% in 2014, for example, following Russia’s occupation of Crimea and the beginning of the war in Donbas. 

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, the share rose again to 74%, before falling to 70.5% in 2023 and 68% in 2024.

This pattern suggests war and acute social stress temporarily increased the number of people who identified as religious, but the increases did not necessarily become permanent. It has not been a straightforward wartime religious revival.
snippet: Polling suggests the war has made Ukrainians more religious. But a closer look at more than two decades of data suggests a more complex picture.
creator: Michael Newton

title: What Counts as Safe AI?
content:
AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and IBM now boast an addition to their AI safety and security credentials: ISO/IEC 42001 certifications.

The certificate confirms that the companies have established a process to identify and manage AI risks. Although it does not guarantee that OpenAI’s ChatGPT will always produce accurate answers, that Anthropic’s Claude cannot be misused, or that Alphabet’s Gemini is free from bias, it gives nervous corporate customers something valuable: evidence that an outside auditor has examined a company’s AI management and meets the standard.

That’s enough to turn ISO 42001 into AI’s first global trust mark.
snippet: AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and IBM now boast an addition to their AI safety and security credentials: ISO/IEC 42001 certifications.
creator: Anda Bologa

title: Panicked Putin Reaches for Nationalization Button
content:
Vladimir Putin has signed a decree allowing the state to seize refineries, telecom companies, and retail outlets if their owners fail to adequately protect against drone attacks. The threat of nationalization by a regime with a fondness for the Soviet era is generating fear among Russian businessmen and oligarchs.

According to the decree, almost every element of critical infrastructure, including private enterprises that are deemed crucial for the country’s security and the economy, can be “temporarily” taken into government ownership for an indefinite period.

Few doubt that the decision was a panicked response to recent Ukrainian drone attacks on oil facilities, which have caused a massive gasoline crisis, and on at least 21 warehouses belonging to Wildberries, a Russian version of Amazon, that have already killed at least 14 civilians and caused widespread fear.

title: NATO’s Missing Link: Shielding Vulnerable Infrastructure
content:
A new railway is not a strategic capability if it ends at a vulnerable bridge. A battery is not a reserve if it relies on the substation whose loss it is meant to bridge. A second data center is not redundancy if both sites share a fiber route, supplier, or control layer. Such assets do not necessarily create strategic capability.

Recent US intelligence assessments reportedly warn that Russia may test NATO’s resolve between next month and 2029. NATO must be sure that the civilian infrastructure its forces depend on will work under pressure.

At the 2025 Hague Summit, allies agreed that up to 1.5% of GDP (of the total defense spending pledge of 5%) may include key national infrastructure and resilience. NATO has since approved a €27bn ($32bn) plan for improved fuel storage and distribution, for example, while the European Commission estimates that electricity grids need more than €1.2 trillion by 2040.

title: Europe’s Next Tech Target: Child Safety
content:
When European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her State of the Union address in mid-September, the Brussels tech community will focus on her promised proposals to keep children safe. It’s the highest-profile tech dossier on her agenda, overshadowing both the bloc’s antitrust crackdown and artificial intelligence regulation. 

What von der Leyen will announce remains unclear. She could call for a complete ban on under-13s or under-16s accessing social media. Or she could opt for a partial restriction. Her proposal could be limited to social media or extended to potentially all other types of Internet platforms, from messaging devices to online marketplaces.  

How Europe plans to achieve age gating represents another unanswered question. Will each website or app be required to verify birthdates? Or will that responsibility fall on Apple, Google, and Microsoft, who operate dominant app stores and operating systems? 

Expect close judicial scrutiny. France’s top court recently struck down a ban on social media for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression. Will Europe’s other courts make similar objections? France has since banned mobile phones in schools.
snippet: When European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her State of the Union address in mid-September, the Brussels tech community will focus on her promised proposals to keep children safe.
creator: Bill Echikson
